Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(D\) be the set of positive divisors of \(250\):

\[
D=\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250\}.
\]

We will show that the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]

---

## 1. Structure forced on the sets \(A_d\), \(d\mid 250\)

First note that putting \(i=j\) in the given condition gives

\[
|A_i|=\gcd(i,i)=i.
\]

Also, if \(a\mid b\), then

\[
|A_a\cap A_b|=\gcd(a,b)=a=|A_a|,
\]

so

\[
A_a\subseteq A_b.
\]

For \(e,f\in D\), let \(g=\gcd(e,f)\). Since \(g\mid e,f\), we have \(A_g\subseteq A_e\cap A_f\). But

\[
|A_e\cap A_f|=\gcd(e,f)=g=|A_g|,
\]

so in fact

\[
A_e\cap A_f=A_g.
\]

Now define, for each \(d\in D\),

\[
N_d=A_d\setminus \bigcup_{\substack{e\mid d\\ e<d}} A_e.
\]

We claim that the sets \(N_d\) partition \(A_{250}\).

Take any \(x\in A_{250}\), and let \(m(x)\) be the smallest divisor of \(250\) such that \(x\in A_{m(x)}\). If \(x\in A_d\) for some \(d\in D\), then

\[
x\in A_{m(x)}\cap A_d=A_{\gcd(m(x),d)}.
\]

By the minimality of \(m(x)\), we must have \(\gcd(m(x),d)=m(x)\), so \(m(x)\mid d\). Thus

\[
x\in A_d \iff m(x)\mid d.
\]

Also, \(x\notin A_e\) for any proper divisor \(e\) of \(m(x)\), so \(x\in N_{m(x)}\). Hence the \(N_d\) are disjoint and

\[
A_{250}=\bigsqcup_{d\in D} N_d.
\]

Moreover, for each \(d\in D\),

\[
A_d=\bigsqcup_{e\mid d} N_e.
\]

Therefore

\[
|A_d|=\sum_{e\mid d}|N_e|.
\]

But \(|A_d|=d\), and the standard identity

\[
\sum_{e\mid d}\varphi(e)=d
\]

shows that

\[
|N_d|=\varphi(d).
\]

Thus the sizes are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
|N_d| & 1&1&4&4&20&20&100&100
\end{array}
\]

---

## 2. Relabeling \(A_{250}\) as \(\{1,2,\dots,250\}\)

The condition is invariant under any bijective relabeling of positive integers. Since \(A_{250}\) has exactly \(250\) elements, we may relabel its elements as \(1,2,\dots,250\) in increasing order, and send all other elements to integers larger than \(250\). This does not increase any of the quantities \(\max A_d\) for \(d\mid 250\).

So we may assume

\[
A_{250}=\{1,2,\dots,250\}.
\]

Now each integer \(t\in\{1,\dots,250\}\) belongs to a unique set \(N_d\). Write \(c_t=d\). For each \(d\in D\), let

\[
L_d=\max\{t:c_t=d\}
\]

be the last position occupied by elements of \(N_d\).

Since

\[
A_d=\bigcup_{e\mid d}N_e,
\]

we have

\[
\max A_d=\max_{e\mid d} L_e.
\]

We need to minimize

\[
S=\sum_{d\in D}\max_{e\mid d}L_e.
\]

---

## 3. Reduction to a scheduling problem

Suppose \(e\mid d\), and in the sequence of labels some copy of \(d\) appears before some copy of \(e\). Swapping those two labels does not increase \(S\).

Indeed, for any fixed divisor \(x\mid 250\):

- If \(d\nmid x\), then the later occurrence of \(e\) moves earlier, so the maximum for \(x\) cannot increase.
- If \(d\mid x\), then both \(e\) and \(d\) divide \(x\), so the two relevant positions remain present and the maximum is unchanged.

Therefore, without increasing \(S\), we may assume that whenever \(e\mid d\), all copies of \(e\) appear before all copies of \(d\).

In such an ordering, for every \(d\in D\),

\[
\max A_d=L_d.
\]

Now order the divisors by their last occurrences:

\[
L_{d_1}<L_{d_2}<\cdots<L_{d_8}.
\]

This order is a linear extension of the divisibility poset. For each \(k\), all copies of \(d_1,\dots,d_k\) have already appeared by position \(L_{d_k}\), so

\[
L_{d_k}\ge \sum_{r=1}^k |N_{d_r}|
=\sum_{r=1}^k \varphi(d_r).
\]

Thus

\[
S\ge \sum_{k=1}^8 \sum_{r=1}^k \varphi(d_r).
\]

Equivalently, we must minimize the sum of completion times for eight jobs with processing times

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
\varphi(d) & 1&1&4&4&20&20&100&100
\end{array}
\]

subject to the precedence condition that if \(e\mid d\), then job \(e\) must be scheduled before job \(d\).

---

## 4. The optimal schedule

We use the standard adjacent-swap fact: if two adjacent incomparable jobs \(X,Y\) have processing times \(p_X>p_Y\), then scheduling \(Y\) before \(X\) lowers the total completion time by \(p_X-p_Y\).

Since \(1\) precedes everything and \(250\) follows everything, we only need to order

\[
2,5,10,25,50,125.
\]

### Claim 1: \(2\) comes before \(5\)

If \(5\) came before \(2\), the only jobs that could appear between them are \(25\) and \(125\). Moving job \(2\) left across such jobs gives adjacent swaps of the form

\[
(25,2)\quad\text{or}\quad(125,2),
\]

which decrease the total completion time because \(20>1\) and \(100>1\). Finally, swapping \(5\) and \(2\) decreases the total because \(4>1\). Contradiction.

So the schedule must begin

\[
1,2,5.
\]

### Claim 2: \(10\) comes before \(25\)

After \(1,2,5\), if \(25\) came before \(10\), the only job that could appear between them is \(125\). Moving \(10\) left across \(125\) and then across \(25\) decreases the total completion time because \(100>4\) and \(20>4\). Contradiction.

So the schedule must begin

\[
1,2,5,10,25.
\]

### Claim 3: \(50\) comes before \(125\)

After \(1,2,5,10,25\), the only remaining jobs before \(250\) are \(50\) and \(125\). Since \(20<100\), \(50\) must come before \(125\).

Thus the unique optimal order is

\[
1,\;2,\;5,\;10,\;25,\;50,\;125,\;250.
\]

The corresponding completion times are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
C_d & 1&2&6&10&30&50&150&250
\end{array}
\]

Hence

\[
S\ge 1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

---

## 5. Construction attaining 499

For every positive integer \(m\), choose a set \(C_m\) of size \(\varphi(m)\), with all \(C_m\) disjoint. For \(m\mid 250\), assign

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1&=\{1\},\\
C_2&=\{2\},\\
C_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
C_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
C_{25}&=\{11,\dots,30\},\\
C_{50}&=\{31,\dots,50\},\\
C_{125}&=\{51,\dots,150\},\\
C_{250}&=\{151,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(m\nmid 250\), choose \(C_m\) to consist of distinct integers larger than \(250\), disjoint from all the other \(C_m\).

Now define

\[
A_i=\bigcup_{m\mid i} C_m.
\]

Then for any \(i,j\),

\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{m\mid \gcd(i,j)} C_m,
\]

so

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|
=\sum_{m\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(m)
=\gcd(i,j).
\]

For the divisors \(d\mid 250\), the maxima are exactly the completion times above:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max A_1&=1,\\
\max A_2&=2,\\
\max A_5&=6,\\
\max A_{10}&=10,\\
\max A_{25}&=30,\\
\max A_{50}&=50,\\
\max A_{125}&=150,\\
\max A_{250}&=250.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
=1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=499.
\]

Thus the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
